expected: No, it was abnormally low: 3,214 pcs over 23–28 Mar (6 working days), against 4,395–4,870 in each of the previous 8 full weeks (mean 4,652.5), about 31% below. The drop started on Wed 25 Mar; 23 and 24 Mar were normal (733, 779).

q: Why did assembly output drop on 25 March?
Something happened to assembly around the 25th. What does the data say?
why did assembely drop on 25th march
expected: The data cannot establish a cause; the log has no downtime, equipment, staffing or material fields. What it shows: assembly fell from 779 (24 Mar) to 394 (25 Mar) and stayed at 394–464 for six working days through 31 Mar. On 25 Mar, knitting (915), washing (801) and packing (658) were all normal or higher, so the drop is confined to assembly and is not caused by a shortage of input. The cause needs to be verified on the floor.

q: Is knitting causing the assembly drop?
Did upstream knitting fall short and starve assembly?
is knittng the reason assembly is low?
expected: No, the data rules that out. Knitting stayed normal or higher during the assembly drop: 829–1,033 from 25 to 31 Mar (mean 932.5, against 895.2 before). Assembly received more input than it could process: over those six days knitting exceeded assembly by 3,042 pcs, against about 120 a day normally, so work is piling up before assembly. The real cause is within assembly and cannot be identified from the log.
